claim: LAST is a c-Myc-inducible long noncoding RNA that cooperates with CNBP to promote CCND1 mRNA stability in human cells.
source: LAST, a c-Myc-inducible long noncoding RNA, cooperates with CNBP to promote CCND1 mRNA stability in human cells
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the title and abstract, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript including knockdown studies, RNA pull-down assays, and stability measurements.

claim: Cyclin D1 is a critical regulator of cell cycle progression and works at the G1 to S-phase transition.
source: Cyclin D1 is a critical regulator of cell cycle progression and works at the G1 to S-phase transition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established scientific knowledge about cyclin D1 function.

claim: LAST binds to the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA to protect against possible nuclease targeting.
source: Mechanistically, LAST was shown to cooperate with CNBP to bind to the 5′UTR of CCND1 mRNA to protect against possible nuclease targeting.
evidence: This mechanism is demonstrated through RNA pull-down assays showing LAST and CNBP binding to the 5'UTR (Figure 4A, B) and stability assays showing protection of CCND1 mRNA.

claim: CCND1 mRNA is not the only target of LAST and CNBP; three additional mRNAs (SOX9, NFE2L1, and PDF) are post-transcriptional targets.
source: In addition, data from CNBP RIP-seq and LAST RNA-seq showed that CCND1 mRNA might not be the only target of LAST and CNBP; three additional mRNAs were shown to be post-transcriptional targets of LAST and CNBP.
evidence: This is supported by RIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing 225 overlapping genes, with experimental verification of SOX9, NFE2L1, and PDF (Figure 5).

claim: Depletion of LAST diminished tumor formation in a xenograft model.
source: In a xenograft model, depletion of LAST diminished and ectopic expression of LAST induced tumor formation, which are suggestive of its oncogenic function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by xenograft experiments showing reduced tumor growth when LAST is knocked down (Figure 6A, B).

claim: Ectopic expression of LAST induced tumor formation in a xenograft model.
source: In a xenograft model, depletion of LAST diminished and ectopic expression of LAST induced tumor formation, which are suggestive of its oncogenic function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by xenograft experiments showing increased tumor growth when LAST is overexpressed (Figure 6C, D).

claim: c-Myc regulates the expression of approximately 10–15% of genes in the genome.
source: Indeed, as a master transcriptional factor, c-Myc regulates the expression of approximately 10–15% of genes in the genome, including a variety of protein-coding genes
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2012; Fernandez et al., 2003.

claim: Cyclin D1 forms a complex with CDK4 or CDK6 and functions as a regulatory subunit whose activity is required for G1/S transition.
source: Cyclin D1 forms a complex with CDK4 or CDK6 and functions as a regulatory subunit whose activity is required for G1/S transition
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Sherr, 1995 and Resnitzky et al., 1994.

claim: Cyclin D1 is a short-lived protein with a rapid turnover rate of approximately 24 minutes.
source: Cyclin D1 is a short-lived protein with a rapid turnover rate (~24 min) due to degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system
evidence: This is cited from Diehl et al., 1998 and Diehl et al., 1997.

claim: Mutation, amplification and overexpression of CCND1 are frequently observed in cancer and contribute to tumorigenesis.
source: Mutation, amplification and overexpression of CCND1 are frequently observed in cancer and have been reported to contribute to tumorigenesis
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wiestner et al., 2007; Elsheikh et al., 2008; Musgrove et al., 2011.

claim: lncRNA-52 (RP11-660L16.2, ENST00000529369) was downregulated when c-Myc expression was suppressed by doxycycline treatment.
source: Two of the five lncRNAs, namely, lncRNA-51 and lncRNA-52, along with CDK4 (positive control) were found to be downregulated when c-Myc expression was suppressed by doxycycline treatment (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A using P493-6 cells with a c-Myc tet-off system.

claim: Knockdown of lncRNA-52 (LAST) showed a significant reduction in colony formation.
source: knockdown of this lncRNA (Figure 1B) showed a significant reduction in colony formation (Figure 1C and D)
evidence: This is demonstrated by colony formation assays shown in Figures 1C and D.

claim: LAST is located approximately 1.8 Mb downstream of the cyclin D1/CCND1 gene in a head-to-tail orientation.
source: lncRNA-52 is located approximately 1.8 Mb downstream of the cyclin D1/CCND1 gene in a head-to-tail orientation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A based on genomic location data.

claim: LAST is approximately 700 nt in length as detected by northern blot analysis.
source: A band of approximately 700 nt in length was detected in both P493-6 and H1299 cells, but was absent in P493-6 cells treated with doxycycline, which suppresses c-Myc expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by northern blot analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: LAST was predominantly localized in the cytosol.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, LAST was predominantly localized in the cytosol.
evidence: This is shown by single molecule RNA FISH in Figure 1F and confirmed by subcellular fractionation in Figure 1G.

claim: The LAST copy number was higher in tumor cells than in normal cells.
source: The LAST copy number was higher in tumor cells than in normal cells (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown by quantitative measurements in Figure 1H comparing normal cell lines (HAFF, IMR90, MCF10A) to tumor cell lines (HCT116, MCF7, H1299).

claim: Lentivirus-mediated gene knockdown of c-Myc decreased LAST expression.
source: Lentivirus-mediated gene knockdown of c-Myc decreased whereas ectopic expression of c-Myc increased LAST expression in HCT116, H1299 and MCF10A cells (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR data shown in Figures 1I and J.

claim: Ectopic expression of c-Myc increased LAST expression.
source: Lentivirus-mediated gene knockdown of c-Myc decreased whereas ectopic expression of c-Myc increased LAST expression in HCT116, H1299 and MCF10A cells (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-PCR data shown in Figures 1I and J.

claim: c-Myc binds to chromatin fragments corresponding to the BS2 and BS3 sites in the LAST gene.
source: The chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay determined the association of c-Myc with chromatin fragments corresponding to the BS2 and BS3 sites (within F2 fragment) among all examined fragments (Figure 1K, lower panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: BS2 and BS3 sites confer c-Myc-dependent transcriptional activity.
source: Luciferase expression from the reporter containing an individual BS2 or BS3 site was indeed induced by ectopic expression of c-Myc (Figure 1L, lower panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Mutant BS2M and BS3M sites showed no response to c-Myc induction.
source: By contrast, mutant BS2M and BS3M sites showed no response to c-Myc induction (Figure 1L, lower panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase reporter assays with mutated binding sites shown in Figure 1L.

claim: c-Myc transactivates LAST.
source: These data demonstrate that c-Myc transactivates LAST.
evidence: This conclusion is based on ChIP assays showing c-Myc binding and luciferase assays showing transcriptional activation.

claim: Knockdown of LAST caused a decrease in the percentage of cells in the S and G2/M phases and an increase in the percentage of cells in the G1 phase.
source: Knockdown of LAST caused a decrease in the percentage of cells in the S and G2/M phases and an increase in the percentage of cells in the G1 phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: LAST promotes G1/S phase transition.
source: As a result, LAST was shown to promote G1/S phase transition.
evidence: This is inferred from cell cycle analysis showing G1 arrest upon LAST knockdown.

claim: Among G1-related cyclins and CDKs genes examined, only the CCND1 mRNA level was significantly decreased upon LAST knockdown.
source: Among all of the mRNAs examined, only the CCND1 mRNA level was significantly decreased (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR analysis in Figure 2A examining multiple cell cycle genes.

claim: Among all cyclins or CDKs examined, only cyclin D1 was downregulated when LAST was depleted.
source: Among all of the cyclins or CDKs examined, only cyclin D1 was shown to be downregulated when LAST was depleted (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by western blot analysis in Figure 2B.

claim: Knockdown of LAST did not change c-Myc expression at either the mRNA or protein levels.
source: we found that LAST, which is also regulated by c-Myc (Figure 1A), does not affect c-Myc stability since knockdown of LAST did not change c-Myc expression at either the mRNA or protein levels (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR and western blot data in Figures 2A and B.

claim: Depletion of LAST decreased cyclin D1/CCND1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Depletion of LAST decreased whereas over-expression of LAST increased cyclin D1/CCND1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in normal HAFF cells and tumor H1299 and HCT116 cells as shown in Figures 2C and D.

claim: Over-expression of LAST increased cyclin D1/CCND1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Depletion of LAST decreased whereas over-expression of LAST increased cyclin D1/CCND1 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in normal HAFF cells and tumor H1299 and HCT116 cells as shown in Figures 2C and D.

claim: LAST showed no effect on either the mRNA or protein levels of adjacent genes DHCR7 and NADSYN1.
source: we checked the shRNA-mediated LAST knockdown effect on the two adjacent genes DHCR7 and NADSYN1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and found that LAST showed no effect on either the mRNA or protein levels of those two genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and excludes cis-acting effects on neighboring genes.

claim: The levels of CCND1 pre-mRNA containing four intronic regions remained unaltered between control and LAST knockdown cells.
source: The levels of CCND1 pre-mRNA containing four intronic regions were found to remain unaltered between control and LAST knockdown cells, whereas the levels of mature spliced CCND1 mRNA containing 5'UTR, CDS (coding sequences) and 3'UTR regions were greatly reduced upon LAST depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B using intron-specific primers.

claim: The levels of mature spliced CCND1 mRNA were greatly reduced upon LAST depletion.
source: The levels of CCND1 pre-mRNA containing four intronic regions were found to remain unaltered between control and LAST knockdown cells, whereas the levels of mature spliced CCND1 mRNA containing 5'UTR, CDS (coding sequences) and 3'UTR regions were greatly reduced upon LAST depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B using exon-specific primers.

claim: LAST post-transcriptionally regulates CCND1 mRNA.
source: These results suggest that LAST may post-transcriptionally regulate CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pre-mRNA levels are unchanged while mature mRNA levels decrease upon LAST depletion.

claim: Knockdown of LAST resulted in a decrease of the half-life of CCND1 mRNA from 5 hr to 3 hr.
source: Knockdown of LAST resulted in a decrease of the half-life of CCND1 mRNA from 5 hr to 3 hr (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is demonstrated by actinomycin D chase experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Over-expression of LAST increased the half-life of CCND1 mRNA from 5 hr to 9 hr.
source: whereas over-expression of LAST increased its half-life from 5 hr to 9 hr (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by actinomycin D chase experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LAST stabilizes CCND1 mRNA.
source: indicating that LAST stabilizes CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is concluded from mRNA half-life experiments showing increased stability with LAST overexpression and decreased stability with LAST knockdown.

claim: Endogenous CCND1 mRNA co-precipitated with LAST in a biotinylated oligonucleotide pull-down assay.
source: as shown in Figure 3C, endogenous CCND1 mRNA but not CCNB1 mRNA co-precipitated with LAST, indicating an association between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA pull-down assay shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There is no complementary base pairing between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.
source: However, by careful inspection, we found there was no complementary base pairing between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of LAST and CCND1 mRNA.

claim: CNBP was identified as a protein that binds to LAST by mass spectrometry.
source: Proteins pulled down by LAST were separated by SDS PAGE, and a unique band with a molecular weight of approximately 20 kDa was revealed and identified as CNBP by mass spectrometry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, left panel).
evidence: This is shown by mass spectrometry analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CNBP has a preference for binding single-stranded DNA and RNA.
source: CNBP has a preference for binding single-stranded DNA and RNA (Flink and Morkin, 1995)
evidence: This is cited from Flink and Morkin, 1995.

claim: CNBP has been reported to function in the translation of ornithine decarboxylase mRNA.
source: and has been reported to function in the translation of ornithine decarboxylase mRNA (Sammons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Sammons et al., 2010.

claim: A biotin-labeled antisense DNA probe against LAST pulled down CNBP, but not cyclin D1.
source: A biotin-labeled antisense DNA probe against LAST pulled down CNBP, but not cyclin D1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, right panel).
evidence: This is shown by pull-down assay in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both CNBP and LAST were coprecipitated when CCND1 mRNA was pulled down using a biotinylated antisense DNA probe.
source: we first pulled down CCND1 mRNA using a biotinylated antisense DNA probe as bait; both CNBP and LAST were coprecipitated (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown by RNA pull-down assay in Figure 3D.

claim: CNBP interacts with both CCND1 mRNA and LAST as shown by RIP assay.
source: The RIP assay further concluded that CNBP interacts with both CCND1 mRNA and LAST (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RIP assay shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CNBP acts as a mediator for LAST and CCND1 mRNA binding.
source: These data demonstrate that CNBP acts as a mediator for LAST and CCND1 mRNA binding.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple pull-down and RIP experiments showing CNBP bridges LAST and CCND1 mRNA.

claim: CNBP knockdown in HCT116 led to a decrease in both the mRNA and protein levels of cyclin D1/CCND1.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, CNBP knockdown in HCT116 led to a decrease in both the mRNA and protein levels of cyclin D1/CCND1.
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR and western blot analysis in Figure 3F.

claim: The half-life of CCND1 mRNA was reduced from 5 hr to 3 hr as CNBP was depleted.
source: The half-life of CCND1 mRNA was reduced from 5 hr to 3 hr as CNBP was depleted (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is demonstrated by actinomycin D chase experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claim: CNBP prolongs the CCND1 mRNA half-life.
source: further demonstrating that CNBP prolongs the CCND1 mRNA half-life.
evidence: This is concluded from mRNA stability experiments showing decreased half-life upon CNBP depletion.

claim: CNBP was co-precipitated by either LAST or CCND1 mRNA in the cytoplasm, but not the nucleus.
source: Using a LAST and CCND1 mRNA pull-down assay, we found that CNBP was co-precipitated by either LAST or CCND1 mRNA in the cytoplasm, but not the nucleus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by subcellular fractionation and pull-down assays in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Knockdown of CNBP affected the level of mature CCND1 mRNA, but not unspliced CCND1 pre-mRNA.
source: Further investigation revealed that knockdown of CNBP affected the level of mature CCND1 mRNA, but not unspliced CCND1 pre-mRNA, indicating that the protective role of CNBP in mature CCND1 mRNA stability occurred in the cytosol since nuclear unspliced CCND1 pre-mRNA was not affected when CNBP was silenced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The increased expression of CCND1 mRNA caused by over-expression of LAST was diminished when CNBP was depleted.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, the increased expression of CCND1 mRNA caused by over-expression of LAST was diminished when CNBP was depleted (lanes 2 vs. 4).
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: LAST affects CCND1 mRNA via CNBP.
source: Thus, our hypothesis is that LAST affects CCND1 mRNA via CNBP.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments showing LAST's effect on CCND1 requires CNBP.

claim: Knockdown of LAST resulted in no change in CNBP at either the RNA or protein levels.
source: Knockdown of LAST resulted in no change in CNBP at either the RNA or protein levels (Figure 3H)
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR and western blot analysis in Figure 3H.

claim: LAST affects CCND1 mRNA not according to the quantity of CNBP, but rather by the association of CNBP and CCND1 mRNA.
source: which suggests that LAST affects CCND1 mRNA not according to the quantity of CNBP, but rather by the association of CNBP and CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that LAST knockdown doesn't change CNBP levels but does affect CCND1 mRNA stability.

claim: Less LAST was co-precipitated when CNBP was depleted in an RNA pull-down experiment starting with the same amount of CCND1 mRNA.
source: An RNA pull-down experiment was performed starting with the same amount of CCND1 mRNA, and less LAST was co-precipitated as CNBP was depleted (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is shown by RNA pull-down assay in Figure 3I.

claim: Less co-precipitated CNBP was detected when the same amount of CCND1 mRNA was pulled down after LAST was silenced.
source: Similarly, when we pulled down the same amount of CCND1 mRNA, less co-precipitated CNBP was detected as LAST was silenced. As a negative control, the RNA-binding protein HuR remained unchanged after LAST was knocked down (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is shown by RNA pull-down assay in Figure 3J.

claim: LAST cooperates with CNBP to regulate CCND1 mRNA stability.
source: These data suggest that LAST cooperates with CNBP to regulate CCND1 mRNA stability.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple experiments showing interdependence of LAST and CNBP in binding and stabilizing CCND1 mRNA.

claim: The 5'UTR but not 3'UTR of CCND1 mRNA was able to bind LAST and CNBP.
source: We found that the 5'UTR but not 3'UTR-1,–2 and −3 of CCND1 mRNA was able to bind LAST and CNBP (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: This is shown by RNA pull-down assays using different CCND1 mRNA fragments in Figures 4A and B.

claim: LAST and CNBP bind to the 5' region of CCND1 mRNA.
source: indicating that LAST and CNBP bind to the 5' region of CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is concluded from mapping experiments showing binding to the 5'UTR.

claim: The half-life of ectopically expressed CCND1 mRNA lacking the 5'UTR was not altered by the presence or absence of LAST and CNBP.
source: The half-life of ectopically expressed CCND1 mRNA lacking the 5'UTR was not altered by the presence or absence of LAST and CNBP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by actinomycin D chase experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The half-life of CCND1 mRNA bearing 5'-UTRs was extended from 4 hr in the absence of LAST and CNBP to 9 hr in the presence of LAST and CNBP.
source: By contrast, the half-life of CCND1 mRNA bearing 5'-UTRs was extended from 4 hr in the absence of LAST and CNBP to 9 hr in the presence of LAST and CNBP, indicating that LAST and CNBP enhanced CCND1 mRNA stability via its 5'UTR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by actinomycin D chase experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LAST and CNBP enhanced CCND1 mRNA stability via its 5'UTR.
source: indicating that LAST and CNBP enhanced CCND1 mRNA stability via its 5'UTR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is concluded from experiments showing the 5'UTR is required for LAST/CNBP-mediated stabilization.

claim: An enrichment peak at the CCND1 5'UTR was observed in CNBP RIP sequencing.
source: In addition, we performed CNBP RIP sequencing, and an enrichment peak at the CCND1 5'UTR was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by RIP-seq data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: LAST, the 5'-UTR of CCND1 mRNA and CNBP form a ternary complex.
source: LAST and CNBP were present in the streptavidin-biotin precipitates (Figure 4C, panel 5 and 6), indicating that these three components indeed form a ternary complex.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequential immunoprecipitation assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CNBP prefers to bind G-rich motifs, especially the GGAG core.
source: CNBP prefers to bind G-rich motifs, especially the GGAG core (Armas et al., 2008; Benhalevy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Armas et al., 2008 and Benhalevy et al., 2017.

claim: Nearly sixty percent of the CNBP enriched sequences contained the GGAG motif.
source: Nearly sixty percent of the CNBP enriched sequences contained the GGAG motif, and more than ninety percent of the peak sequences contained a GGR motif (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown by bioinformatics analysis of CNBP RIP-seq data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: More than ninety percent of the CNBP enriched peak sequences contained a GGR motif.
source: Nearly sixty percent of the CNBP enriched sequences contained the GGAG motif, and more than ninety percent of the peak sequences contained a GGR motif (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown by bioinformatics analysis of CNBP RIP-seq data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: G-rich-1 and G-rich-2 in the CCND1 5'UTR were responsible for the binding of CNBP.
source: An electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) was performed, and the results showed that G-rich-1 and G-rich-2 in the CCND1 5'UTR were responsible for the binding of CNBP (Figure 4D, lower part).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA shown in Figure 4D.

claim: G-rich-A, C, D and F from LAST were able to bind CNBP, whereas neither G-rich-B nor G-rich-E was able to bind CNBP.
source: G-rich-A, C, D and F from LAST were able to bind CNBP, whereas neither G-rich-B nor G-rich-E was able to bind CNBP (Figure 4E, lower part).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CNBP only interacted with G-rich sequences that contained the GGAG core, but not those lacking the GGAG core.
source: Thus, CNBP only interacted with G-rich sequences that contained the GGAG core, but not those lacking the GGAG core.
evidence: This is concluded from EMSA experiments showing binding specificity for GGAG-containing sequences.

claim: Both CCND1 and LAST interact with CNBP via their G-rich motifs containing the GGAG core.
source: These data suggest that both CCND1 and LAST interact with CNBP via their G-rich motifs containing the GGAG core.
evidence: This is concluded from EMSA experiments showing CNBP binding to GGAG-containing G-rich sequences in both LAST and CCND1.

claim: Over-expression of LAST containing only one site mutation led to an increase in the CCND1 mRNA level, whereas over-expression of LAST containing four G-rich site mutations nullified its effect on the CCND1 mRNA level.
source: We found that over-expression of LAST containing only one site mutation led to an increase in the CCND1 mRNA level, whereas over-expression of LAST containing four G-rich site mutations nullified its effect on the CCND1 mRNA level (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR analysis in Figures 4F and G using mutated LAST constructs.

claim: The effect of LAST on CCND1 stability requires at least one of the four functional G-rich motifs.
source: This result indicates that the effect of LAST on CCND1 stability requires at least one of the four functional G-rich motifs.
evidence: This is concluded from mutagenesis experiments showing loss of function only when all four G-rich motifs are mutated.

claim: LAST binds to the CNBP fragment corresponding to amino acids 92–134 (domain 3).
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, we concluded that LAST binds to the CNBP fragment corresponding to amino acids 92–134 (domain 3)
evidence: This is shown by deletion mapping experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The CCND1 5'UTR binds to the CNBP fragment corresponding to amino acids 29–134 (domain 2 + domain 3).
source: whereas the CCND1 5'UTR binds to the CNBP fragment corresponding to amino acids 29–134 (domain 2 + domain 3) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown by deletion mapping experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 225 overlapping genes were found in the intersection of LAST knockdown mRNA-seq and CNBP RIP-seq.
source: The intersection of these two arrays is shown in Figure 5A, and 225 overlapping genes were found (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is shown by Venn diagram analysis in Figure 5A comparing two transcriptome datasets.

claim: 75 genes met the criteria that CNBP-enriched genes must be 4-fold above the input control level.
source: We further narrowed this list down to 75 genes (Supplementary file 2, bold part) based on the criteria that CNBP-enriched genes must be 4-fold above the input control level.
evidence: This is based on filtering criteria applied to the RIP-seq and RNA-seq overlap.

claim: SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF mRNAs were likely to be regulated by LAST, as knockdown of LAST led to a decrease in their levels.
source: Three mRNAs, namely, SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF, were also likely to be regulated by LAST, as knockdown of LAST led to a decrease in their levels (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Knockdown of LAST decreased the half-lives of SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF mRNAs.
source: Experimental verification showed that knockdown of LAST decreased (Figure 5C) whereas over-expression of LAST increased their half-lives (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown by actinomycin D chase experiments in Figure 5C.

claim: Over-expression of LAST increased the half-lives of SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF mRNAs.
source: Experimental verification showed that knockdown of LAST decreased (Figure 5C) whereas over-expression of LAST increased their half-lives (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown by actinomycin D chase experiments in Figure 5D.

claim: CNBP deletion led to a decrease in the mRNA levels of SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF.
source: In addition, CNBP deletion led to a decrease in the mRNA levels of SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is shown by RT-PCR and western blot analysis in Figures 5E and F.

claim: LAST, together with CNBP, can regulate the stabilization of additional mRNAs, such as SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF.
source: These data suggest that LAST, together with CNBP, can regulate the stabilization of additional mRNAs, such as SOX9, NFE2L1 and PDF.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments showing LAST and CNBP affect the stability of multiple mRNAs beyond CCND1.

claim: Knockdown of LAST decreased the tumorigenicity of HCT116 cells in a xenograft mouse model.
source: Knockdown of LAST decreased the tumorigenicity of HCT116 cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is shown by xenograft experiments in Figures 6A and B showing reduced tumor size and weight.

claim: Induction of LAST promoted HCT116 cell tumorigenicity in a xenograft mouse model.
source: By contrast, induction of LAST promoted HCT116 cell tumorigenicity (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is shown by xenograft experiments in Figures 6C and D showing increased tumor size and weight.

claim: The LAST expression levels were higher in tumor tissues than normal tissues in multiple human cancer types.
source: we found that the LAST expression levels were higher in tumor tissues than normal tissues, including the human bladder, breast, colorectal, esophagus, head and neck, kidney, liver, lung, prostate and stomach.
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA dataset shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The CCND1 expression levels were higher in tumor tissues than in normal tissues in multiple human cancer types.
source: In addition, the CCND1 expression levels were higher in tumor tissues than in normal tissues, including the human bladder, breast, cervix, bile duct, colorectal, esophagus, head and neck, kidney, pancreas, stomach and uterus.
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA dataset shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both the LAST and CCND1 expression levels were higher in most tumor tissues than in their normal counterparts.
source: In conclusion, both the LAST and CCND1 expression levels were higher in most tumor tissues than in their normal counterparts (Figure 6E and F, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on TCGA dataset analysis shown in Figures 6E, F and supplementary figures.

claim: LAST promotes tumorigenesis.
source: The above results suggest that LAST promotes tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is concluded from xenograft experiments and TCGA data analysis showing oncogenic properties of LAST.

claim: The absence of LAST downregulated expression of 667 genes in HTC116 cells.
source: The absence of LAST downregulated expression of 667 genes (log2 (fold change) below - 0.58) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is shown by RNA-seq analysis in HCT116 cells with LAST knockdown.

claim: Among the top 10 significant pathways associated with 667 differentially expressed genes upon LAST knockdown, the majority were associated with tumorigenesis.
source: Among these 10 pathways, the majority were associated with tumorigenesis (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is shown by pathway analysis in Figure 6G.

claim: c-Myc can upregulate or downregulate expression of cyclin D1 in a context-dependent manner.
source: c-Myc can upregulate or downregulate expression of cyclin D1 in a context-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by citations showing both activation and repression of CCND1 by c-Myc in different cellular contexts.

claim: c-Myc, together with Max, activates CCND1 transcription through an E box located at −558 nt in its promoter.
source: On the one hand, c-Myc, together with Max, a co-transcription factor, activates CCND1 transcription through an E box located at −558 nt in its promoter (Kress et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Kress et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2011.

claim: Simultaneous overexpression of c-Myc and ZO-2 enhances repression of the CCND1 promoter through the E box in MDCK cells.
source: On the other hand, simultaneous overexpression of c-Myc and ZO-2 enhances repression of the CCND1 promoter through the E box in MDCK cells (Gonzalez-Mariscal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Gonzalez-Mariscal et al., 2009.

claim: c-Myc has been reported to repress the cyclin DI promoter and antagonize USF-mediated transactivation in BALB/c-3T3, Rat6 and rat embryo fibroblasts.
source: In addition, c-Myc has been reported to repress the cyclin DI promoter and antagonize USF-mediated transactivation in BALB/c-3T3, Rat6 and rat embryo fibroblasts (Philipp et al., 1994).
evidence: This is cited from Philipp et al., 1994.

claim: Multiple transcription factors, including AP-1, NF-κB, E2F and Oct-1, can bind to their respective CCND1 promoters and regulate its expression.
source: In addition to c-Myc, multiple transcription factors, including AP-1, NF-κB, E2F and Oct-1, can bind to their respective CCND1 promoters and regulate its expression (Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Guo et al., 2011.

claim: GATA3 cooperates with PARP1 to regulate CCND1 transcription by modulating histone H1 incorporation.
source: GATA3 cooperates with PARP1 to regulate CCND1 transcription by modulating histone H1 incorporation (Shan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Shan et al., 2014.

claim: MYF5-mediated enhancement in CCND1 mRNA translation contributes to early myogenesis.
source: Moreover, post-transcriptional mechanisms are also involved in the regulation of CCND1, as exemplified by MYF5-mediated enhancement in CCND1 mRNA translation, which contributes to early myogenesis (Panda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Panda et al., 2016.

claim: Mutations in CCND1 leading to stable truncated transcripts are associated with increased cell proliferation and shortened survival of cancer patients.
source: Mutations in CCND1 leading to stable truncated transcripts are associated with increased cell proliferation and shortened survival of cancer patients (Wiestner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Wiestner et al., 2007.

claim: Long noncoding RNAs are defined as transcripts that are longer than 200 nucleotides and lack protein coding capacity.
source: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), which are defined as transcripts that are longer than 200 nucleotides and lack protein coding capacity
evidence: This is a standard definition of lncRNAs in the field.

claim: lncRNAs are emerging as important regulators of biological processes, including regulation of gene expression at multiple levels.
source: are emerging as important regulators of biological processes, including regulation of gene expression at multiple levels, such as chromatin remodeling, transcription, and post-transcriptional modulation (Derrien et al., 2012; Iorio and Croce, 2012; Bonasio and Shiekhattar, 2014; Wilusz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references establishing the role of lncRNAs.

claim: c-Myc transcriptionally regulates many lncRNA genes, such as PVT1, the CCAT family, and MYCLos.
source: Genome-wide studies have shown that c-Myc transcriptionally regulates many lncRNA genes, such as PVT1, the CCAT family, and MYCLos
evidence: This is cited from Colombo et al., 2015; Nissan et al., 2012; Ling et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2015a; Kim et al., 2015b.

claim: A number of lncRNAs have been demonstrated to be important components of the c-Myc-mediated signaling network.
source: whereas a number of lncRNAs have been demonstrated to be important components of the c-Myc-mediated signaling network (Colombo et al., 2015; Nissan et al., 2012; Ling et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2015a; Kim et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: Lacking LAST causes cell cycle arrest at the G1/S stage due to decreased cyclin D1.
source: Lacking this lncRNA causes cell cycle arrest at the G1/S stage due to decreased cyclin D1 and attenuates tumor growth.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell cycle analysis and cyclin D1 measurements upon LAST knockdown.

claim: Lacking LAST attenuates tumor growth.
source: Lacking this lncRNA causes cell cycle arrest at the G1/S stage due to decreased cyclin D1 and attenuates tumor growth.
evidence: This is demonstrated by xenograft experiments showing reduced tumor formation upon LAST depletion.

claim: LAST could be a potential target for new cancer therapeutics.
source: Conceivably, LAST could be a potential target for new cancer therapeutics.
evidence: This is speculated based on LAST's oncogenic function and role in tumor growth.

claim: There was no correlation between the expression levels of CCND1 and LAST in the 15 tumor types examined.
source: However, a correlation between the expression levels of CCND1 and LAST in the 15 tumor types examined was not found (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA data.

claim: There was no difference in survival when tumors were divided into those expressing high versus low CCND1 or LAST.
source: In addition, there was no difference in survival when tumors were divided into those expressing high versus low CCND1 or LAST.
evidence: This is based on survival analysis of TCGA data.

claim: The regulation of CCND1 is more complicated than anticipated.
source: These results imply that the regulation of CCND1 is more complicated than we had anticipated, and new functions of LAST need to be characterized.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between LAST and CCND1 expression in tumors and lack of survival differences.

claim: CNBP acts on cap-independent translation of ornithine decarboxylase mRNA.
source: Previous studies have shown that CNBP acts on cap-independent translation of ornithine decarboxylase mRNA (Sammons et al., 2010)
evidence: This is cited from Sammons et al., 2010.

claim: CNBP functions in sterol-mediated transcriptional regulation as well as c-Myc transcription.
source: and also functions in sterol-mediated transcriptional regulation as well as c-Myc transcription (Rajavashisth et al., 1989; Murphy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Rajavashisth et al., 1989 and Murphy et al., 2009.

claim: CNBP is able to guide lncRNA to bind to the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA, acting as a mediator between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.
source: CNBP is able to guide lncRNA to bind to the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA, acting as a mediator between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by multiple pull-down and RIP experiments showing CNBP bridges LAST and CCND1 mRNA.

claim: lncRNAs are able to regulate their genomic neighborhoods in cis.
source: lncRNAs are able to regulate their genomic neighborhoods in cis (Quinn and Chang, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Quinn and Chang, 2016.

claim: Examples of cis-acting lncRNAs include enhancer RNAs (eRNAs), imprinted lncRNAs and dosage compensation lncRNAs.
source: Examples of cis-acting lncRNAs include enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) (De Santa et al., 2010), imprinted lncRNAs (Mancini-Dinardo et al., 2006; Sleutels et al., 2002) and dosage compensation lncRNAs (Lee, 2012; Conrad and Akhtar, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references.

claim: CCND1 and LAST are both located on chromosome 11, and the two genes are 1.8 Mb apart and in the same transcriptional direction (+strand).
source: Homo sapiens cyclin D1/CCND1 and LAST are both located on chromosome 11, and the two genes are 1.8 Mb apart and in the same transcriptional direction (+strand).
evidence: This is based on genomic location data.

claim: CCND1 and LAST do not share the same promoter but are transcribed separately by c-Myc via their respective promoters.
source: It is interesting to note that although CCND1 and LAST are both subjected to positive transcriptional regulation by c-Myc, they do not share the same promoter. Rather, CCND1 and LAST are transcribed separately by c-Myc via their respective promoters (Figures 1K and 6H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP assays and shown in the model in Figure 6H.

claim: The relatively long distance between the CCND1 and LAST genes may preclude their direct interaction.
source: The relatively long distance between the CCND1 and LAST genes may preclude their direct interaction.
evidence: This is speculated based on the 1.8 Mb distance between the genes.

claim: LAST borrows a trans-acting factor, CNBP, as a mediator to connect the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA and itself.
source: Moreover, LAST was shown to borrow a trans-acting factor, CNBP, as a mediator to connect the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA and itself, thus affecting CCND1/cyclin D1 expression in trans.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing CNBP mediates the interaction between LAST and CCND1 mRNA.

claim: Without CNBP, LAST shows no effect on CCND1.
source: Without CNBP, LAST shows no effect on CCND1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), further supporting the concept that LAST does not regulate CCND1 in cis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: LAST does not regulate CCND1 in cis.
source: further supporting the concept that LAST does not regulate CCND1 in cis.
evidence: This is concluded from the requirement of CNBP for LAST's effect on CCND1 and the lack of direct interaction.

claim: Co-location of CCND1 and LAST on the same chromosome appears to be a random event.
source: Therefore, co-location of CCND1 and LAST on the same chromosome appears to be a random event.
evidence: This is speculated based on the trans-acting mechanism and lack of cis regulation.

claim: LAST interacts with CNBP, by which it is guided towards the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA, leading to the stabilization of CCND1 mRNA.
source: Normally, LAST interacts with CNBP, a RNA binding protein, by which it is guided towards the 5'UTR of CCND1 mRNA, leading to the stabilization of CCND1 mRNA, which in turn ensures orderly cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on all experimental data.

claim: In the case of LAST dysregulation, CCND1 mRNA becomes unstable, resulting in decreased cyclin D1, inevitably causing cell cycle arrest and stoppage of cell division.
source: In the case of LAST dysregulation, CCND1 mRNA becomes unstable, resulting in decreased cyclin D1, inevitably causing cell cycle arrest and stoppage of cell division (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is the proposed model shown in Figure 6H based on experimental observations.

claim: This is a novel mechanism for CCND1 mRNA regulation.
source: This is a novel mechanism for CCND1 mRNA regulation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the novelty of the lncRNA-mediated 5'UTR protection mechanism.

claim: The lack of similarity between human LAST and transcripts of Mus musculus precludes using mouse c-Myc-driven tumor models to further clarify the significance of LAST in c-Myc-mediated cell cycle regulation and tumor growth in vivo.
source: The lack of similarity between human LAST and transcripts of Mus musculus also precludes using mouse c-Myc-driven tumor models to further clarify the significance of the LAST in c-Myc-mediated cell cycle regulation and tumor growth in vivo (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 6I.

claim: NcRNACCND1 was reported to negatively regulate CCND1 transcription by recruiting TLS to the CCND1 promoter.
source: Very recently, NcRNACCND1 was reported to negatively regulate CCND1 transcription by recruiting TLS to the CCND1 promoter (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Wang et al., 2008.

claim: Pitx2 and HuR, which belong to the same ribonucleoprotein complex, control the decay rate of CCND1 mRNA.
source: Moreover, Pitx2 and HuR, which belong to the same ribonucleoprotein complex, also control the decay rate of CCND1 mRNA (Gherzi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Gherzi et al., 2010.

claim: The G1/S transition is a major checkpoint in cell cycle progression, as it is a 'point of no return' beyond which cells are committed to dividing.
source: The G1/S transition is a major checkpoint in cell cycle progression, as it is a 'point of no return' beyond which cells are committed to dividing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: Cyclin D1, along with its catalytically active partner CDK4, is a positive cell cycle regulator that advances the cell cycle from G1 to S phase.
source: Cyclin D1, along with its catalytically active partner CDK4, is a positive cell cycle regulator that advances the cell cycle from G1 to S phase (McKay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from McKay et al., 2002.

claim: The lncRNA PVT1 is known to be a c-Myc regulated lncRNA that is involved in c-Myc stability and activity.
source: The lncRNA PVT1 is known to be a c-Myc regulated lncRNA that is involved in c-Myc stability and activity (Colombo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Colombo et al., 2015.

claim: Unlike PVT1, LAST does not affect c-Myc stability.
source: However, unlike PVT1, we found that LAST, which is also regulated by c-Myc (Figure 1A), does not affect c-Myc stability
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing no change in c-Myc levels upon LAST knockdown.

claim: The oncoprotein c-Myc plays a pivotal role in multiple cellular processes, such as cell cycle progression, malignant transformation, differentiation suppression and apoptosis induction.
source: The oncoprotein c-Myc plays a pivotal role in multiple cellular processes, such as cell cycle progression, malignant transformation, differentiation suppression and apoptosis induction, predominantly through its transcription activity (Seth et al., 1993; Drayton et al., 2003; Wei et al., 2003; Demeterco et al., 2002; Prendergast, 1999; Amati et al., 1992; Lee et al., 1996; Hoffman and Liebermann, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from multiple references establishing c-Myc's role.

claim: Cyclin D1 interacts with the tumor suppressor pRB1, which in turn positively regulates cyclin D1 expression.
source: Cyclin D1 also interacts with the tumor suppressor pRB1, which in turn positively regulates cyclin D1 expression (DeGregori, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from DeGregori, 2004.

claim: The Skp2 F-box protein is involved in cyclin D1 degradation.
source: While early studies showed that the Skp2 F-box protein is involved in cyclin D1 degradation (Yu et al., 1998)
evidence: This is cited from Yu et al., 1998.

claim: Two additional F-box proteins play important roles in targeting cyclin D1 for proteasome degradation.
source: a recent study has identified two additional F-box proteins that play important roles in targeting cyclin D1 for proteasome degradation (Lin et al., 2006; Okabe et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from Lin et al., 2006 and Okabe et al., 2006.
